---
title: "Comparison at matched disclosure"
subtitle: "3.7 · eight simulated units; frontier after the postrank theory book, ch. 16"
description: "Excess expected wrong counts relative to a frontier at each rule's disclosure."
---

Rules that disclose different numbers of pairs need not be comparable by expected wrong count alone. At each rule's
own disclosure, the frontier gives the smallest expected count attained by a report in the family or by a mixture
of two complete reports. The vertical difference measures excess expected errors at that disclosure. The display
also identifies the best single report when the same count is attainable without randomisation. A rule outside the
specified family retains its evaluated risk but receives no frontier comparison within that family.

## Numerical illustrations {#what-to-try}

- **Same N, τ .20.** Posterior-mean tiers state 21 pairs with E 3.114. The frontier is 2.951, a gap of .1634.
  The mixture prints the more-disclosing report with chance .667; the best single report at that N has E 3.013.
- **Estimate tiers.** Three tiers from the estimates also state 21 pairs, but their gap is .6429.
- **Flags.** The flag report states 19 pairs and lies on the frontier: gap 0.
- **Strict order, τ .05.** Stating all 28 pairs leaves a gap of .2305. The cross marks risk above all-withheld at
  this τ; changing τ does not change this rule's gap.
- **At most three grades.** Among 6,051 reports, the estimate tiers' gap becomes .4796. The posterior-mean tiers
  reach the capped frontier, where only balanced reports with sizes three, three and two attain the endpoint.
- **Four tiers outside the cap.** The rule is outside this family and receives no benchmark. The all-withheld
  rule remains available in the select, at N 0.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
Every rule uses one supplied teaching posterior; postrank does not fit it. The flags use the mean of all thirty
league estimates, even on these eight units. A frontier mixture averages complete reports: each realised report
states one endpoint's N. Its error fraction is a ratio of expected counts, not an average of realised fractions.
The gap assesses this loss and disclosure, not the purpose for which a rule was designed.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="In postrank"}

The package's synthetic `pr_example_gaussian` poverty example uses its own thirty sites. At τ .25 with at most four
grades, this prints quantile cuts with N 337 and risk .1758, versus optimal cuts with N 303 and risk .1603. The risks correspond to different N; H(m) is not a package output.

```r
w <- c(poverty=1, frl=0, snap=0); s <- postrank_settings(weights=w, tau=.25, G_max=4L); sc <- pr_example_gaussian$means[, "poverty"]
sapply(c("quantile", "optimal"), function(r) unlist(postrank_cuts(sc, pr_example_gaussian, s, direction="descending", rule=r)$evaluation[c("N", "primary_risk")]))
```

:::
